title: Time Passes · 8
paragraphs: She meant no harm by it. The family wouldn’t come, never again, some said, and maybe the house would be sold at Michaelmas, the autumn quarter day. So Mrs. McNab bent down and picked a bunch of flowers to carry home. While she dusted, she set them on the table. She liked flowers. It seemed a shame to let them go to waste. Say the house was sold (and she stood, hands on hips, before the looking glass)—well, it would need seeing to, that it would. All these years it had stood there with nobody in it. The books and things were moldy, what with the war and help being so hard to come by; the place hadn’t been cleaned the way she’d have wanted. It would take more than one pair of hands to set it right now. She was too old for it. Her legs hurt. Every one of those books ought to be laid out on the grass in the sun; plaster had come down in the hall; the drainpipe over the study window had got blocked and let the rain in; the carpet was completely ruined. But people should come and see for themselves; they should’ve sent someone down to look. There were clothes in the cupboards, after all; they’d left clothes in every bedroom. What was she meant to do with them? The moth was in them—Mrs. Ramsay’s things. Poor lady! She’d never need _them_ again. She was dead, they said; years ago, in London. Here was the old gray cloak she used to garden in (Mrs. McNab ran her fingers over it). She could see her now, as she came up the drive with the washing, bent over her flowers (a pitiful sight the garden was now, run wild, rabbits scuttling out at you from the beds)—could see her in that gray cloak with one of the children by her side. There were boots and shoes; there was a brush and comb left lying on the dressing table, for all the world as if she meant to be back tomorrow. (She’d died very sudden at the end, they said.) Once they’d been going to come, but they put it off, what with the war and traveling being so hard these days; and all these years they’d never come; only sent her money; never wrote, never came, and expected to find everything just as they left it, ah dear! Why, the drawers in the dressing table were stuffed full (she pulled them open)—handkerchiefs, scraps of ribbon. Yes, she could see Mrs. Ramsay, as she came up the drive with the washing.

She had such a nice way with her. All the girls took to her. But dear me, a great deal had changed since those days (she shut the drawer); plenty of families had lost the ones they loved best. So she was dead; and Mr. Andrew killed; and Miss Prue gone too, so they said, with her first baby; but these years everybody had lost somebody. Prices had gone up something shocking, and they never came down again, neither. Oh, she remembered her well, in that gray cloak.

“Good evening, Mrs. McNab,” she’d said, and told cook to put by a plate of milk soup for her—quite sure she’d be wanting it, after lugging that heavy basket all the way up from town. Mrs. McNab could see her this minute, bent over her flowers. (And, faint and flickering, like a yellow beam of light or the circle at the far end of a telescope, a lady in a gray cloak, bent over her flowers, went drifting across the bedroom wall, up over the dressing table and across the washstand, while Mrs. McNab hobbled and shuffled about, dusting and tidying.)

And what was cook’s name, now? Mildred? Marian?—something of that sort. Ah, it had gone—she did forget things. A fiery one, the way red-haired women are. Many’s the laugh the two of them had had. There was always a welcome for her in the kitchen. She made them laugh, she did. Things were better then than they are now.

She sighed; it was too much work for one woman. She wagged her head from side to side. This room had been the nursery. Why, it was damp right through in here; the plaster was coming down. Whatever did they want with an animal’s skull hung up there? Gone all moldy, too. Rats in every attic, and all. The rain got in. But they never sent word; never came. Some of the locks had gone, so the doors kept banging. She didn’t care to be up here on her own at dusk, neither. It was too much for one woman—too much, too much. She creaked, she groaned. She banged the door shut. She turned the key in the lock and went, leaving the house shut up, locked, alone.
